blocks.raw: <Callout>Biophilic design reconnects occupants to nature through direct and indirect patterns, enhancing psychological well-being and reducing stress. The Terrapin Bright Green framework provides 14 replicable patterns applicable to Philippine architecture, from water features in tropical courtyards to biomimetic ceiling patterns reflecting indigenous natural geometry.</Callout>

blocks.raw: <Tip>Terrapin's 14 Patterns collapse into three memorable categories: *Nature In* (direct elements—water, plants, animals), *Nature As* (patterns and materials mimicking nature—spirals, fractals, wood texture), *Nature Of* (spatial relationships—prospect/refuge, heights, enclosure). This three-part structure is testable and helps organize 14 patterns that otherwise seem disparate.</Tip>

blocks.raw: <Note>Biophilic design is *not* "add plants to building." Decorative potted plants without integration into ventilation, daylighting, or spatial hierarchy are expensive gardening, not biophilic strategy. Effective biophilic integration serves functional or thermal purposes (water features provide evaporative cooling; vegetation screens provide shade; natural materials reduce acoustic harshness). This functional integration distinguishes genuine biophilic design from cosmetic green-washing.</Note>

blocks.raw: <Warn>Critical distinction: biophilic water features are NOT simple fountains. In Type II (no dry season) and Type IV (year-round moisture) climates, standing water risks mosquito breeding and fungal growth. Effective biophilic water strategy in perpetually moist climates requires: (1) moving/cascading water preventing stagnation, (2) drainage systems preventing pooling, (3) maintenance protocols ensuring water clarity. Static water features in Type II/IV zones are environmental hazards, not biophilic design—confusing this is a major LEA error.</Warn>
